title: Should Homework Be Banned?
description: Four recordings about homework: a radio discussion, two students talking, a parent-teacher meeting and a talk about research.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio discussion
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Karen, talking to a head teacher, Mr Davies, about homework.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: Today's debate: should homework be banned in primary and secondary schools? With me is Mr Davies, a head teacher whose school stopped setting homework two years ago. Mr Davies, that's a bold move.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: It was, Karen, and we had plenty of worried parents at first. But we looked at the research, and it showed that for younger children, homework makes almost no difference to progress.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: Almost none? That surprises me.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: It surprised us, too. What matters far more is the quality of lessons. Meanwhile, homework was causing arguments at home, and some children from busy or crowded households simply couldn't do it. That created an unfair gap.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: And have results suffered since you made the change?

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Not at all. They've stayed level, and attendance has even improved slightly, which suggests the children are happier.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: But isn't homework a way of teaching responsibility?

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: In theory, yes. In practice, many parents ended up doing the work for their children, so what was being taught was something rather different.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: So what do the children do in the evenings now?

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: We encourage them to read for pleasure, play, help at home, and sleep. And I should be honest: we do keep a little homework for the oldest pupils, because exams are coming and they need to practise independently.

script.speaker: Karen
script.text: So it isn't a complete ban.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: No, and I'd never claim it was. It's more a question of balance.

parts.title: Part 2 · Two students
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Nam and Mai, talking about their homework.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I can't believe how much homework we got today. Maths, a history essay, and a chemistry report, all due by Friday.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Welcome to my life. I did five hours last night. Five! I hardly ate dinner.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Five hours? Surely it doesn't take you that long.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: It does when you're trying to do it properly. Honestly, I think some of it is pointless. Like when our English teacher asks us to copy out a whole page.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I don't mind that one so much, but the maths is useful. If I didn't do the exercises at home, I'd never remember the formulas.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That's a fair point. Practice is different from busywork. But my concern is that I've stopped playing the violin because I'm too tired.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's a shame. Could you talk to Mr Tran? He's quite reasonable.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I might. Last term, he cut the homework for the whole class after we all complained, remember?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: True. Perhaps if we write a polite letter, rather than moaning, he'll listen.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Good idea. Shall we draft it this evening, or is that too much homework?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Ha! Let's do it at lunch tomorrow.

parts.title: Part 3 · A parent and a teacher
parts.intro: You will hear a parent, Mrs Clarke, talking to her son's teacher, Mr Tran.

script.speaker: Mr Tran
script.text: Thank you for coming in, Mrs Clarke. I wanted to talk about Oliver's homework.

script.speaker: Mrs Clarke
script.text: Yes, I wanted to raise that too. He's in tears at least twice a week, and I don't think it's because he's lazy.

script.speaker: Mr Tran
script.text: I don't think so either. He's one of the most capable students in the class. The problem is that he's very perfectionist. He'll spend an hour on a ten-minute task.

script.speaker: Mrs Clarke
script.text: That's exactly what I see. He rewrites whole paragraphs because one word looks wrong.

script.speaker: Mr Tran
script.text: In that case, I'd suggest a time limit. Tell him that after thirty minutes on any task, he stops, whatever the state of the work. I'll write a note in his diary so that I know it's deliberate and he doesn't lose marks.

script.speaker: Mrs Clarke
script.text: That would be a relief. And what about the weekend project? It's due on the same day as his piano exam.

script.speaker: Mr Tran
script.text: I hadn't realised. Let's move the project to the following Monday. I'd rather he did two things well than three badly.

script.speaker: Mrs Clarke
script.text: Thank you, that's very kind. I was worried you'd say I was making excuses for him.

script.speaker: Mr Tran
script.text: Not at all. Parents who tell me early make my job much easier. Please email me if anything else comes up.

parts.title: Part 4 · A talk about research
parts.intro: You will hear Dr Reyes giving a talk about what research says on homework.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Good evening. I'd like to summarise what research says about homework, because the public debate often runs ahead of the evidence.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: First, the age of the student matters enormously. In primary schools, studies find only a weak link between homework and achievement. In secondary schools, the link is stronger, particularly for moderate amounts, about one to two hours a night.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Notice the word moderate. Beyond about two hours, extra homework no longer helps and may even harm results, because tired students learn less and become stressed.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Second, type matters. Tasks that ask students to review something taught that day, or to practise a skill, tend to be effective. Tasks that are simply long, or that require expensive equipment, tend not to be.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: I should add that most of these studies are observational, which means they show a link, not a cause. Good teachers may both set better homework and produce better results, so we must be careful about drawing strong conclusions.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Third, and this is often overlooked, we should ask who benefits. Students with a quiet room and supportive parents gain the most. Students without those advantages gain the least, so homework may widen inequality rather than reduce it.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: So should it be banned? My honest view is no, but it should be rethought. Shorter, purposeful tasks, offered with support at school, such as homework clubs, would probably give better results than either extreme.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Thank you. I'm happy to take questions.

Why many teachers are leaving the profession
How homework should be marked fairly
How a new school should be designed
